title: Francis and the birds
hook: a rich man's son gives it all away and preaches to the birds, who stay to listen (Little Flowers 16)

segments.voice: Yesterday, take and read: a child's voice in a Milan garden, and one verse. Your line was our heart is restless. Where did you ask, why not now? Day ninety-three.

Picture the town square in Assisi, a hill town in Italy, around the year 1206. A crowd has gathered in front of the bishop. A rich cloth merchant is furious with his son, Francis, who has been giving away the family's money and goods to rebuild a ruined chapel and to feed the poor. The father wants it all back. And Francis, in front of everyone, takes off his clothes, every piece, folds them, and hands them to his father. From now on, he says, I can say freely, our Father who art in heaven. The bishop wraps him in his own cloak. The party boy of Assisi walks out of town with nothing. And some years later, on a road in the Umbrian countryside, he stops, because the trees are full of birds.
screen: `A FATHER, A SON, A BISHOP.` → `HE HANDS BACK HIS CLOTHES.` → `TREES FULL OF BIRDS.`

segments.voice: The story is told in the Little Flowers of Saint Francis, a collection written down about a century after his death, and earlier by his first biographer, Thomas of Celano. Francis tells his companions, wait for me here, I'm going to preach to my little sisters, the birds. And he walks into the field and talks to them. He tells them they owe God a lot of praise: for their feathers, for the freedom to fly anywhere, for rivers and springs to drink from, for food they never had to plant or harvest, echoing Jesus's words about the birds of the air. And the story says the birds stay. They open their beaks, stretch out their necks, bow their heads, and don't fly away until he blesses them. Then they rise and scatter in four directions, like a cross. Historians read the Little Flowers as memory mixed with loving legend, and nobody can say exactly what happened in that field. But the heart of it matches everything else we know about Francis. For him the whole world was family. Near the end of his life, sick and nearly blind, he wrote a song of praise in his own Italian dialect, often called one of the first great poems in the Italian language. It's called the Canticle of the Creatures, and it praises God for brother sun, and sister moon and the stars, brother wind, sister water, brother fire, and our sister, mother earth. At the very end, he even welcomes sister death. Francis's feast day is October fourth, and many churches bless animals on or near it. A pope in our own time took his name, and titled a letter about caring for the earth with the canticle's refrain, praised be you.
screen: `MY LITTLE SISTERS, THE BIRDS.` · `THE BIRDS STAY TO LISTEN.` · `MEMORY MIXED WITH LEGEND.` · `THE CANTICLE OF THE CREATURES.` · then, large: `BROTHER SUN, SISTER MOON.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: watch a bird for one minute. If you can, go to a window or step outside. Find a bird, any bird: a pigeon counts, a sparrow counts, a crow on a wire counts. If there are none, watch a tree, or the sky. Just watch. How it moves its head. How it lands. Don't name it or photograph it. Let it be your brother or sister for a minute. If you pray, you can praise God for it, the way Francis did. If you don't, just be glad it exists. The bell holds the time.
Francis and the birds. The rich man's son who gave everything back, and called every creature family.
Your line: brother sun, sister moon. Today, greet one part of creation as family: the sun on your face, the rain, the moon tonight. Tomorrow, a nun who laughed. Day ninety-three.

howItsDone: Saint Francis's feast day is October 4, and many Catholic, Anglican and Lutheran churches hold a blessing of the animals on or near it. A hymn based on his Canticle of the Creatures, 'All Creatures of Our God and King', is sung in many churches.

fork.setup: you're Francis, walking with your companions. the trees beside the road are full of birds. what do you do?
options: walk on. there's a town to preach in.
tell your friends to wait, and go and preach to the birds.
fork.reveal: he tells his companions to wait, and preaches to his little sisters the birds, who, the story says, stay to listen.

trapdoor: what you thought: a sweet garden statue of a monk with a bird.
what it means: a rich man's son hands back everything he owns and treats all of creation, even the birds, as his brothers and sisters.
what a scholar hears: the bird sermon is told by Thomas of Celano and in the later Little Flowers; the Canticle, written in Umbrian around 1225, is among the earliest poems in Italian.

notes: Date of the renunciation before the bishop: usually 1206; stated as 'around the year 1206'.
'From now on I can say freely, our Father who art in heaven' paraphrases the early lives (Celano, Bonaventure); not quoted. Confirm.
The Little Flowers are treated as memory mixed with legend; the Celano reference for the bird sermon should be checked (First Life, section 58).
Canticle of the Creatures: c. 1225; 'one of the first great poems in the Italian language' is a common claim; confirm.
Pope Francis (2013) and the encyclical Laudato si' (2015) are alluded to without naming; confirm this is acceptable on the broad Christian path.
'All Creatures of Our God and King' is W. H. Draper's paraphrase of the Canticle; it is named but not quoted.

Review fix: the script had said Laudato si' takes the canticle's 'first words'; the canticle opens 'Altissimu, onnipotente, bon Signore', and 'Laudato si'' is its repeated refrain. Changed to 'refrain, praised be you'. Confirm the English gloss.
'One of the first great poems in the Italian language' softened to 'often called'; 'party boy of Assisi' reflects Celano's account of his youth. Confirm tone.
